items.title: This 3-step method to simplify your life starts with your obituary
items.description:
Jim VandeHei, Mike Allen, and Roy Schwartz want you to think deeply about death. 
 Not in a morbid sense, mind you. Rather, imagine you’re writing your own obituary. What do you want it to say? 
 “Thinking about it that way and then working backwards really does create a map [for how to spend your time],” VandeHei told Big Think.

items.title: The gap between knowing better and doing better, and how to close it
items.description:
Most of us can recite the benefits of exercise, gratitude, and patience while doing none of it. Tal Ben-Shahar calls this the Knowing-Doing gap, and our typical interventions, like retreats and month-long overhauls keep it open. 
 This video  The gap between knowing better and doing better, and how to close it  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Misery is an emotional feature, not a glitch in the system
items.description: Tolstoy’s famous opening to  Anna Karenina  (1878) about happy families being all alike but unhappy ones each being unhappy in their own way applies just as well to feelings. There are simply more ways to feel bad than to feel good — and more words to describe those bad feelings. English is bloated with terms for anger, anxiety, sorrow, shame, jealousy, regret. items.title: Ask Ethan: How did atoms come to be?
items.description: At the core of everything we’ve ever touched, seen, or interacted with here on Earth is the same humble physical structure: the atom. items.title: The information paradox at the heart of every black hole
items.description: When something falls into a black hole, where does the material ultimately go, and will it, or the quantum information that it contained, ever come back out again? According to Einstein’s general relativity, those answers are simple: as soon as anything physical — matter, antimatter, radiation, etc. — crosses over the event horizon, it’s irretrievably gone. items.title: Scientists map massive layer of life just beneath our feet
items.description:
Directly beneath our feet stretches a world both smaller and much, much larger than the one we know. Scientists have just begun mapping what may well be the largest piece of infrastructure on Earth: a network of fungal threads that is 68  quadrillion  miles long.

items.description:
